en: The Sūtra of King Aśoka, Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabara of Funan during the Liang Dynasty. Part One:
The Causes and Conditions of Birth. Chapter One: The Causes and Conditions of Birth.
The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
Rising early in the morning, he dressed, took up his bowl,
and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms, surrounded by a community of bhikṣus.
At that time, a verse was spoken from the midst of space:
“The Buddha’s body is like a mountain of gold; His gait is like that of an elephant king.
His countenance is exceedingly dignified and serene, Just like the full moon.”
Surrounded by a retinue of bhikṣus, he entered the city together with them.
At that time, as the World-Honored One was about to enter the city and his foot stepped upon the threshold of the gate,
various inconceivable wonders occurred.
The blind regained their sight;
the deaf were able to hear;
the mute were able to speak.
The lame are able to walk;
those imprisoned and confined all attain liberation;
and those who harbor enmity and hatred all give rise to loving-kindness and compassion.
The calf, its bonds naturally loosened, went to its mother;
all the beasts—elephants, horses, oxen, and the like—were filled with great joy and all let out loud roars.
All the birds—parrots, śārikas, kalaviṅkas, peacocks, and others—warbled their songs in harmony.
Various ornaments, such as bracelets, armlets, hairpins, and earrings, along with diverse precious objects within chests and caskets, spontaneously emitted sounds.
It was exceedingly delightful;
all manner of music spontaneously played together,
and at that time, this earth naturally became pure.
It was free from all impurities, evils, gravel, pebbles, stones, thorns, and poisonous weeds;
it shook in six ways,
surging up in the east and subsiding in the west.
It surged up in the west and sank in the east;
it surged up in the south and sank in the north;
it surged up in the north and sank in the south.
The center surged upward while the four sides sank;
the four sides surged upward while the center sank.
It revolved in circles, manifesting these various and extraordinary wonders.
At that time, a verse was further spoken from the sky:
"The entire great earth, with the four seas as its garment, Adorned by kingdoms, cities, and various mountains—
When the World-Honored One treads upon the ground, It quakes in six ways."
Just as a ship upon the ocean is driven by the wind,
so when the Buddha enters the city,
he causes all people to give rise to joy and exultation through his supernormal powers.
Just as the waters of the great ocean are stirred by the wind,
all the people spoke these verses:
"Nothing in this world is more delightful than the Buddha’s entry into the kingdom."
The great earth shook in six ways; all sand and gravel were swept away without remainder.
Those with impaired sense faculties all attained full perfection.
All kinds of musical instruments spontaneously produced wondrous sounds.
The Buddha’s light illuminates all lands, like a thousand suns shining upon the world;
Sprinkling fragrant water upon the ground and scattering sandalwood powder,
At that time, this city was the foremost among all adorned realms.
At that time, as the World-Honored One proceeded along the main road,
there were two young boys on the road.
One was a son of the Hārgalokulīśa (translated as "Most Victorious Clan").
The first was a son of the Śyāma clan (literally "long-treading" or "victory-clan"), whose name was Jaya (literally "victory").
These two boys were playing in the sand;
the first boy was named Jaya.
The second boy was named Vijaya, which translates as "Unconquerable.
When these two boys saw the World-Honored One’s body with its thirty-two marks,
the first boy took sand and ground it into flour, which he then held up and offered into the Buddha’s alms bowl.
The second child joined his palms in sympathetic joy and spoke this verse:
"Spontaneously great compassion, A body adorned with a halo."
Having already distanced myself from birth and death, I now contemplate with single-minded devotion;
because I recollect the Buddha with my mind, I offer this sand as an act of worship.
At that time, after Jayā had made her offering, she made this aspiration:
"By this root of goodness, may I become a sovereign king of a single umbrella over the earth and extensively make offerings within the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha, knowing his mind, beheld his right aspiration.
In future ages there will be supreme and wondrous fruits,
because the Buddha-Tathāgata serves as a field of merit; thus,
with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, he accepted this sand.
Even as he smiles, his body emits various rays of light—
blue, yellow, red, and white—
which may issue forth from the crown of his head.
Or light may emerge from beneath his knees;
this light illuminates the eight hells,
so that those who are cold obtain warmth and those who are hot obtain coolness.
The light illuminated their bodies, and all their suffering and affliction were eliminated.
Those sentient beings felt doubt and wonder in their hearts, thinking,
"I have already been liberated from suffering."
"Does he remain right here,
or is he reborn in another place?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to inspire a wholesome thought, further manifested a transformed person.
He causes them to arrive at that place.
Upon seeing it, those sentient beings give rise to the thought, saying:
"We have not been born in a different place."
"By the power of this person alone, I have been liberated from suffering.
Furthermore, as he gave rise to such thoughts toward the transformed person,
his karmic retributions for hell were entirely extinguished.
When their lives there have ended, they are reborn in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) among humans or devas where the truths can be realized.
From the crown of their heads, light radiates forth, illuminating everything from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Within that light, they proclaim the teachings on suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self.
Again, he spoke in verse:
"One should diligently leave the household life And, in accord with the Buddha-dharma,
Destroy the army of birth and death, Just as an elephant destroys a house."
If a person applies themselves diligently to the Buddha-dharma without negligence,
abandoning all saṃsāra, they shall attain the extinction of all suffering;
the Buddha’s radiance can illuminate the trichiliocosm.
Having shone forth, they re-enter the Buddha’s body.
If the Buddha wishes to prophesy karmic retribution from the past, the light enters through his back;
if he wishes to prophesy karmic retribution from the future, the light enters through his front.
If the Buddha intends to prophesy rebirth in the hells, light enters through his feet;
if he intends to prophesy rebirth among animals, light enters through his ankles;
if he intends to prophesy rebirth as a hungry ghost, light enters through his toes.
If the Buddha intends to prophesy the birth of a human being, light enters through his knees;
if he intends to prophesy the birth of an Iron-Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), light enters through his left palm;
if he intends to prophesy the birth of a Gold-Wheel-Turning King, light enters through his right palm.
If the Buddha intends to prophesy the birth [of a being], light enters through his navel;
if he intends to prophesy the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, light enters through his mouth;
if he intends to prophesy the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, light enters through the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa.
If the Buddha wishes to bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon a bodhisattva,
light issues from his uṣṇīṣa; if it returns to the trichiliocosm,
it first circumambulates the Buddha three times and then enters according to its respective destination.
Now the Buddha smiled, and light issued from his body;
it circled him three times and entered through his left palm. This did not occur without cause or condition.
At that time, having seen this, Ānanda joined his palms in reverence.
And he spoke in verse:
"The Buddha has eliminated pride and the like; He extinguishes enmity and accomplishes the supreme cause.
It is not without cause that he smiles, His teeth as white as jade or snow."
Through wisdom, he knows the matters that others delight to hear;
with the most supreme radiance, he is able to extinguish their doubts.
The Buddha’s voice thunders like a roll of thunder, and his eyes are like those of a bull-king.
"The supreme field of merit for humans and devas— please record the karmic reward for this gift of sand.
The Buddha said,
"Ānanda," [and so forth].
I do not smile without cause.
For a specific reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has manifested this smile.
Ānanda, do you see that child who, with his hands, scoops up sand and places it into the bowl?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Indeed, I have seen it,
World-Honored One. The World-Honored One spoke again:
"This child, one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa,
shall be born in the city of Pāṭaliputra as a king named Aśoka;
he will be a Cakravartin of the four quarters who has faith and delight in the True Dharma."
"You shall extensively make offerings to the relics by erecting eighty-four thousand stūpas for the benefit of many people.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata further spoke in verse:
"After I have entered parinirvāṇa, you shall be born into the Kauśika clan."
He was named King Āyusmanta; delighting in the Dharma, his fame spread far and wide.
By means of my *śarīra* stūpas, he adorned Jambudvīpa;
this was the karmic reward for his merit, having offered sand as a gift to the Buddha.
The Buddha then took some sand and gave it to Ānanda, saying to him,
"Take cow dung, mix it with this sand, and smear it on the ground where the Buddha walks.
Ānanda received the instruction and immediately used it to smear the ground.
...down to the city of Pāṭaliputra.
There was a king named Candragupta (translated as "Moon-Protected").
At that time, the king had a son named Bindusāra (translated as "Firm Reality").
The eldest son of Bimbisāra was named Susīma, translated as "Good Bond.
At that time, a brahmin from the city of Campā gave birth to a daughter whose beauty and features were the foremost in the kingdom.
The physiognomist predicted:
"The husband of this woman shall become a king, and she shall give birth to two sons.
The first son shall become a Cakravartin King who rules over four continents."
The second son left the household life and attained the Way.
Upon hearing these words, the brahmin was filled with great joy;
desiring wealth and honor, he took his daughter and went to the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
Adorning her body with every kind of ornament,
she addressed King Bhīṣmaka, saying,
"My daughter is of such exquisite beauty that she is the foremost in the entire kingdom."
She became the king's consort,
and the king immediately took her into his palace.
All the women of the inner quarters thought to themselves:
"This girl is so exceptionally beautiful that she is the most outstanding in the entire kingdom.
If the King were to see her, he would surely become infatuated with her and cease to love us.
Having reflected thus, the women of the inner quarters [spoke].
Even though he had been made a barber to shave the king's hair,
on one occasion when the king ordered him to shave his hair,
the king fell asleep while the shaving was being performed.
When the king awoke from his sleep, joy arose in his heart,
and he spoke these words to him:
"Whatever you require, speak it according to your wish."
She then said to the king,
"I wish to enjoy myself together with you.
At that time, the king spoke these words.
"You are a barber and I am a king; how can we be the same?
He replied to the king again, saying:
"I am a Brahmin woman, not a barber.
That Brahmin originally intended for me to become the King's consort.
The King then asked again:
"Who appointed you as a barber?
He replied,
"The ladies of the inner apartments."
The king spoke again, saying,
"Do not do such a thing ever again.
He then took her and made her his queen.
After a short time, she conceived and gave birth to a son after ten months.
At that time, the king thought to himself,
"I am now free from sorrow."
He immediately named this son Aśoka, which translates as "Sorrowless" (An-You).
When the second son was born,
because he removed the sorrow from his heart, he named this son Viśoka, which translates as "Remover of Sorrow."
His body was coarse and rough, and his father did not hold him in affection.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, wishing to examine which of his sons was fit to succeed him, summoned an outsider fortune-teller.
The name Piṅgalavatsa translates as "Tawny Calf. He spoke in the language [of the region], saying:
"Upādhyāya, I wish to examine the princes;
after my passing, who is fit to be king?"
Piṅgalavatsa replied, "Great King,
you who wish to see the prince should enter the golden hall.
Thus, King Bimbisāra was led to the golden hall.
Then King Aśoka’s mother said to him, "Great King, today you wish to examine your sons;
you may go there. Aśoka replied:
"The King does not favor me;
how can I go there?
Her mother said to her:
"You may go now. Aśoka replied, "I shall do as you command.
I pray that my mother will send someone with food to that place."
Eventually, when Aśoka departed from the city of Pāṭaliputra,
there was a high minister named Rākṣasa.
Upon meeting Aśoka, he asked,
"Where do you intend to go now?
Aśoka replied:
"Today the Great King intends to examine his sons upon the golden terrace.
I shall go there now.
Then Chenghu (Saṃgharakṣita) gave the most excellent state elephant to Aśoka to ride.
Aśoka mounted an elephant and proceeded to the Golden Palace.
Upon arrival, he sat upon the ground amidst the various kings.
All the kings possessed diverse foods and drinks served in vessels of gold and silver.
At that time, Aśoka’s mother immediately sent someone to prepare rice and curd,
which she placed in earthenware vessels and delivered to Aśoka.
Then, King Bindusāra spoke to the physiognomist, saying:
"You should examine the princes in succession to see who among them is fit to be king after my passing.
Thus did the physiognomist reflect.
"If you say that Aśoka is fit to be king,
the king will not honor him and will surely kill me.
Having reflected thus, he addressed the king, saying, "I shall now describe him by means of his causal signs, without mentioning his name."
The king replied, "Very well.
The physiognomist then said,
"If among the princes there is one who possesses an excellent mount, he shall be fit to be king."
The Great King spoke again,
"You may examine him further.
The physiognomist replied once more.
"If this superior seat is fit for a king," the Great King spoke again,
"you may exchange it once more."
The physiognomist spoke again, saying,
"One who possesses excellent food and drink as well as fine vessels is fit to be a king.
When the princes heard these words, each of them reflected upon them individually.
"If there were someone who possessed a fine carriage, food, and drinking vessels, I would become king.
King Aśoka reflected:
"Now this physiognomist has not mentioned my name; he speaks only on account of my physical marks."
"If one who rides such vehicles as these is fit to be a king, then my vehicle is the most excellent.
Furthermore, I sit upon the great earth, and my food and curd are the finest;
my vessel is made of earth, and I take water as my drink."
"As I see it, I shall become king.
At that time, the physiognomist inquired after his mother's welfare,
and his mother asked him:
"After the Great King has passed away, who shall become king?
He replied, "Aśoka.
He then spoke again to the physiognomist.
If the king should further inquire who is fit to be king,
you should depart to a distant place and not remain here.
If Aśoka obtains the kingship, you may return again.
At that time, the physiognomist traveled far to another country.
At that time, the kingdom ruled by King Bimbisāra was named Takṣaśilā;
it intended to rebel and would not obey the king’s transformation through his influence.
King Bimbisāra said to Aśoka,
"You should assemble the fourfold army and go to that kingdom;
provide them with no weapons or supplies whatsoever."
Eventually, Aśoka led his fourfold army out from the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
The people addressed Aśoka, saying,
"We currently possess neither weapons nor provisions."
"How then shall one be able to subdue and punish that kingdom?
Aśoka replied,
"If there are meritorious qualities, the weapons and provisions required for a king will emerge spontaneously."
Having spoken these words,
the earth immediately split open,
and weapons and provisions emerged all at once.
At that time, Aśoka led the fourfold army to punish Takṣaśilā.
When the people of Takṣaśilā heard that Aśoka was coming,
they went out for half a yojana to adorn the road.
They sprinkled fragrant water upon the ground to welcome Aśoka and said:
"We welcome Your Majesty not for the sake of strife,
nor do we harbor any ill will toward that great king."
"However, the ministers dispatched by the King who reside in my country govern without the Way.
I wish to depose them.
At that time, the people made offerings to Aśoka with various ritual implements.
He was welcomed into the kingdom;
thus it is told at length.
At that time, King Aśoka dispatched an envoy to the country of Kāśī.
In the kingdom of Khasa, there were two powerful men who said to their king,
"The two of us have the strength to level mountains."
"That Aśoka has come; he is not fit to serve as a minister.
At that time, the devas raised their voices and declared, "Aśoka shall become a Cakravartin king divided into four parts and rule over Jambudvīpa."
It was irreversible.
At that time, King Bindusāra’s eldest son, Susīma,
returned from the park and entered the city of Pāṭaliputra.
At that time, the king’s chief minister, Bimbisāra, whose head was hairless,
came out from within the city and encountered [the Buddha] on the road;
wishing to play a private joke, he patted him on the head with his hand.
At that time, the minister reflected and said:
"He is now striking me with his hand;
when he becomes king, you shall harm me with a sword."
"We should employ skillful means so that he shall not become king in the future.

At that time, the minister caused the five hundred ministers to distance themselves from Śuśrūṣaka and said, "Aśoka shall become a Cakravartin King divided into four parts; we should all serve him together."
Eventually, the people of Takṣaśilā rebelled against this great king and no longer remained his subjects.
King Bimbisāra dispatched Susīma to go and punish them.
At that time, though Rūpasvāmin reached that place, he was unable to inflict punishment.
Meanwhile, King Aśoka returned to his own country, where King Bindusāra fell gravely ill and his life was about to end.
The imperial decree was issued: "Send Ārya Śrīya to the kingdom of Takṣaśilā once more, and order him to bring Śiṃha back quickly.
I now wish to entrust the affairs of state to him."
At that time, the ministers smeared yellow ginger juice on Aśoka’s body to simulate the appearance of illness.
They then boiled the juice of the *lakṣā* plant—which has no known Chinese equivalent—and placed it in a bowl; setting it aside in one spot, they announced that Aśoka was ill.
At that time, while King Bindusāra was still alive,
the ministers adorned Aśoka and brought him to the Great King,
addressing him thus:
"This prince is the one whom the Great King ought to invest with the royal throne.
If Śyāma practices asceticism, I shall restore the royal throne to him.
When the Great King heard these words, his heart was filled with great anger and resentment.
Then Aśoka said,
"If I shall rightfully become king,
may the gods immediately grant me a celestial crown."
Having spoken these words, the devas immediately placed celestial crowns upon his head.
Upon seeing this, the Great King’s anger redoubled;
consequently, warm blood issued from his mouth, and he died instantly.
Aśoka then ascended the throne.
Having ascended the throne, he appointed Skandagupta as his chief minister.
At that time, Śuṣima heard that the great king had passed away and Aśoka had taken the throne; he conceived a great hatred.
He immediately set out with his troops intending to punish Aśoka.
At that time, King Aśoka dispatched a large force from within the city to guard its four gates.
He ordered two brave and powerful generals to lead their respective divisions to defend the southern and western gates.
Furthermore, he ordered the minister Rākṣasa to lead the troops to guard the northern gate of the city,
while King Aśoka himself led the troops to guard the eastern gate.
By various skillful means, the minister Rākṣasa constructed mechanical devices at the eastern gate of the city.
They carved wood to represent the body of King Aśoka and his various military hosts;
they dug pits in the ground, filled them with smokeless fire, and covered them with materials,
further placing dry earth upon them.
At that time, Śrīṣeṇa led his troops intending to attack the north gate.
Siṃhagupta said to him, "Do not attack me; you should attack the east gate.
If you can kill King Aśoka, I shall surrender myself."
Then Śūrpakārṇa followed his advice;
he immediately turned his army toward the eastern gate,
but saw that the mechanical men were all motionless.
Thereupon, he went straight forward and fell into a fire pit, burning himself to death.
After Śūrpāraka had died,
there was a military commander there.
His name was Bhadra, translated as "Worthy," and Yodhaka, translated as "Subduer. Possessing great power and valor, he led a host of troops numbering more than a thousand.
Having left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma, he immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, while King Aśoka was governing the affairs of state, five hundred ministers conceived feelings of contempt toward him.
King Aśoka then spoke to those ministers.
"You should cut down the flowering and fruit-bearing trees to protect the thorny ones.
The ministers replied, "Great King, it is not so;
you should cut down the thorny trees to protect the flowering and fruit-bearing trees."
King Aśoka spoke again, saying, "It shall not be so;
you must cut down the flowering trees and preserve the thorny ones.
When he had spoken thus three times, the ministers still did not obey his command.
King Aśoka, filled with rage, immediately drew his sword and severed the heads of five hundred ministers.
Later, on another occasion, King Aśoka took five hundred court ladies into the rear garden.
In the garden there was a tree named Aśoka; when its flowers and leaves bloomed, King Aśoka saw them and said, "This tree shares my name," and for this reason he rejoiced.
At that time, King Aśoka’s body was coarse and rough, so the women did not wish to draw near him.
While the women were sleeping in the royal garden, they acted because they wished to cause the king displeasure.
They stripped the tree of its flowers and leaves until nothing remained.
When King Aśoka awoke and saw that there were no flowers or leaves, he asked his daughters,
"Who has stripped all the flowers from the tree?"
The women replied, "This is what we did.
King Aśoka became enraged and immediately had the women enclosed within bamboo screens and burned them with fire.
Because of his cruelty, the people of that time called him Caṇḍa-Aśoka-rāja; *caṇḍa* translates as "fearsome" (*kewei*).
The minister Siṃhala addressed King Ajātaśatru:
"Regarding such acts as beating or killing, these should be entrusted to others and not performed by you yourself.
The king then issued a proclamation seeking someone capable of carrying out the execution.
At that time, there was a village within the mountains,
and in that village lived a man skilled in the craft of weaving who fathered a son.
His father named him Giri, which translates as "Mountain."

That person is to be feared; capable of practicing non-benevolence, he constantly reviles his parents and beats all the men and women in the household, even going so far as to kill every living being without exception.
He constantly made his living by catching [animals] with nets;
because he killed so many, people further called him Caṇḍagirika, which translates as "Terrifying Mountain.
The king was searching for a wicked man and encountered him.
The messenger said to him, "The King now wishes to govern the people through execution.
Are you able to do this?
The man replied, "I am capable of doing so as to cause all those within Jambudvīpa to be completely slaughtered."
The messenger returned and reported what he had been told to the Great King.
The King immediately said, "Bring this man here.
Having received these instructions, the messenger went to him and said, "The King commands you to come."
He replied to the messenger, saying, "Wait a moment; I must first see my parents. He then informed his parents:
"The Great King Aśoka intends to govern people through universal execution and has commanded me to carry this out. I now wish to depart."
Because his parents did not permit him, the man became angry and killed them; he then returned to the place where the messenger was.
The messenger said to him, "Why have you come so late?
The man replied, "My parents would not allow me to come."
After I have killed him, I shall go to the king's presence and say to the Great King:
"One who wishes to punish people should construct a prison;
the gates of the prison should be adorned and made exceedingly magnificent."
Those who saw him could not help but feel affection and joy.
He further addressed the king, saying, "I request that Your Majesty issue a strict decree that no one who enters prison shall ever be allowed to leave.
The king replied, "Very well."
At that time, Caṇḍagirika went to the Kukkuta Monastery.
Inside the monastery, there was a bhikṣu reciting a sūtra,
and within that sūtra, the matters of the hells were described.
This refers to various forms of suffering, such as boiling cauldrons, glowing embers, mountains of knives, and trees of swords.
If there are those born in hell, they are punished according to their offenses.
This is explained at length, as described in the *Sūtra of the Five Messengers*, regarding the matters of hell.
At that time, having heard these words, Caṇḍakīlika followed them all in preparing the instruments for hell.
At that moment, there was a merchant leader in the city of Śrāvastī who, together with his wife, had entered the ocean.
Upon reaching the sea, he gave his son the name Sāgara (Sea).
For twelve years, he traveled back and forth across the ocean.
One day, he encountered five hundred bandits who killed this merchant leader and plundered his wealth; only the son escaped unharmed.
Later, he left the household life to enter the Buddha’s Dharma.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
Having arrived, he rose early, donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
Because he did not know [the full extent of the realm], he saw the gates of hell adorned with various ornaments;
he then entered therein desiring to beg for alms.
Having entered, he saw the various instruments of torture and immediately wished to leave.
When Caṇḍagirika saw him, he seized him and said, "Now you shall receive death; you shall not escape.
At that time, the bhikṣu was filled with fear and wept, his tears flowing down.
The Caṇḍakīlika spoke in this language:
"For what reason do you weep now like a small child?
The bhikṣu replied: "It is not that I cherish this body; rather, it is because the opportunity to encounter liberation is so difficult to find."
"Renunciation is difficult to attain, yet I have now attained it;
the appearance of Śākyamuni is difficult to encounter, yet I have already encountered him.
However, I have not yet attained the true Dharma within the Dharma; for this reason, I am distressed."
Candagirika said to the bhikṣu,
"I have received the command of the Great King that no one who enters this prison shall ever leave.
At that time, the bhikṣu wept and said, "You must grant me one month."
He replied, "A month is not permitted; it may be granted for seven days.
The bhikṣu, reflecting that death was near, applied himself with diligent vigor until the seven days were complete.
At that time, a prince was conversing with a woman of the inner apartments, and when King Aśoka saw them, he became filled with rage and resentment.
He immediately ordered that these two men be cast into prison to be punished.
Caṇḍagirika then placed the two of them inside an iron mortar and pounded them with a pestle.
Upon seeing this, the bhikṣu was struck with deep terror.
Then he spoke these verses:
The Great Teacher, the Buddha, out of compassion,
This foremost of sages has correctly taught that this form Is like a mass of bubbles— unreal and impermanent.
This body is beautiful in form; where does its cessation lead?
Therefore, one should abandon this dharma cherished by the deluded.
Understanding this, I shall know: liberation lies within this very prison.
"By relying on this, one shall cross over to the shore beyond the three realms of existence.
At that time, during the course of a single night,
the bhikṣu applied himself with diligence and contemplation to sever all afflictions.
He immediately attained the fruit of arhatship.
Cāṇḍakīrī said to the bhikṣu:
"This night has passed and the light of dawn has appeared."
"The time for experiencing suffering has arrived; you should know this.
The bhikṣu replied, "I do not understand what you have said now.
That night had already passed and the light of dawn had appeared.
I alone am able to know for myself that the night of ignorance has passed and the sun of wisdom has appeared.
By the light of the sun of wisdom, I see that all worlds are entirely devoid of reality.
Therefore, I now wish to gather all the world with the Buddha-dharma.
He said to Caṇḍakīlika, "I shall now do with this body of mine whatever you desire.
At that time, the jailer, devoid of compassion and blind to the ways of the world,
became greatly enraged and placed the bhikṣu inside an iron cauldron.
They fill [a cauldron] with thick blood, excrement, urine,
and various impurities, and cook this bhikṣu therein with much firewood;
even when the wood is exhausted, his body does not rot or decay.
At that time, seeing that [the fire] was no different [than before], the warder of the prison became enraged and struck and scolded the jailers:
"Why do you not provide more fire now?
The warder then personally provided firewood and fire, yet the fire would not ignite.
Having seen that it was not burning, he looked into the cauldron and saw this bhikṣu sitting cross-legged upon a lotus flower.
Having witnessed this sight, he immediately went and informed the king.
When the king heard this, he went with all his subjects to see it.
At that moment, the bhikṣu, by means of his supernormal powers, emerged from the iron cauldron in a single thought-moment and ascended into the air.
It was as if a king of swans were soaring through the air, manifesting eighteen miraculous transformations.
At that time, King Aśoka saw this bhikṣu like a mountain split asunder, poised in mid-air.
With a heart full of joy, he spoke this verse:
"Your body is like that of a human being, Yet your spiritual power exceeds that of humans.
I do not know this matter; Who are you now?"
"Therefore, you should speak correctly; you ought to let me know this.
If I come to know this matter, I shall become your disciple.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
This king is now able to accept the Buddha’s words;
he shall extensively construct stūpas and make offerings to the śarīra for the sake of benefiting all people through the Dharma.
Having reflected thus, wishing to manifest his merit, he spoke these verses:
The Buddha has extinguished all outflows; He possesses incomparable great compassion.
Supreme Master of Discourse, I am his disciple;
Possessing the inexhaustible power of the True Dharma, The Buddha, the Bull among Men, is unattached to all existence;
Having disciplined himself, he further disciplines others.
May I now attain liberation from the prison of the three realms of existence.
Furthermore, Great King, as the Buddha has prophesied:
"One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa..."
In the city of Pāṭaliputra,
there shall be a king named Aśoka who will become a Cakravartin King of the Four Quarters;
he will extensively make offerings to my relics.
He erected eighty-four thousand stūpas.
Furthermore, Great King, the prison established by the king was equal to the hells;
within this prison, countless beings were slaughtered.
"Your Majesty should eliminate [this] and bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
Great King, you should now fulfill the intention of the World-Honored One.
Then he spoke in verse:
Therefore, O Great King, you should give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings; by bestowing fearlessness,
you shall fulfill the intention of the World-Honored One and extensively erect stūpas for his relics.
At that time, King Aśoka gave rise to a mind of mindfulness of the Buddha;
with palms joined in repentance, he spoke these verses:
"I take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, And in the disciples of the World-Honored One."
You, son of the One of Ten Powers, should now give rise to a mind of patience;
I confess all the evil deeds I have committed before you.
Now you should cultivate diligence and give rise to a heart of profound reverence.
I adorn this ground with various stūpas,
as white as conch shells or snow, just as the Buddha has taught.
The bhikṣu replied, "Excellent!"
He immediately returned to his dwelling by means of supernatural power.
At that time, King Aśoka desired to leave the prison,
and Caṇḍagirika joined his palms and said:
"Great King,
you should know that once I have accepted my command, none of those who enter this prison shall emerge.
Then the king said, "Do you intend to kill me now?"
He replied, "It is so.
The king asked, "Among us, who entered first?
Caṇḍagirika replied, "I entered first."

Then the king said to the jailers, "Seize Caṇḍakīlika and place him in a *laṅkā-kuṭī*—a term for which there is no equivalent translation—and burn him with fire; furthermore, have men destroy this prison."
Bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings, the king then conceived the desire to extensively construct Buddhist stupas.

He arrayed his fourfold army and proceeded to the site where King Ajātaśatru had erected a stupa, named Thūluna (translated as "Inverted Vase"). Upon arriving, he ordered men to demolish the stupa and take the Buddha’s relics.
In this manner, proceeding in succession, he obtained relics from all seven stupas.
He then went to a village named Rāma, where there was another stupa that had been erected first.
Furthermore, wishing to break it open to retrieve the śarīra, there was at that time a nāga king who immediately led Aśoka into the nāga palace and addressed the king, saying:
"This stūpa is my offering; Your Majesty should leave it here."
The king immediately granted his permission; the nāga king then took Aśoka to the village of Rāma.
At that time, the king reflected that this stūpa was the foremost, and for this reason, the nāga king protected it all the more.
I did not obtain any śarīra relics from this stūpa.
Having completed my reflections, I returned to my own country.
At that time, King Aśoka fashioned eighty-four thousand precious caskets and distributed the śarīra relics throughout these caskets.
Furthermore, he fashioned eighty-four thousand jars as well as various banners and canopies,
and entrusted them to the yakṣas, commanding them to erect stūpas everywhere across the entire earth, reaching even to the great oceans.
Furthermore, it is said that there are three kinds of kingdoms: small, medium, and large.
If a kingdom produces ten million taels of gold, a stūpa for a single King should be erected there.
At that time, such was the case with the kingdom of Takṣaśilā.
He brought forth thirty-six million taels of gold.
The people of that kingdom said to King Aśoka,
"Your Majesty, you should grant us thirty-six caskets."
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately reflected: "I wish to construct many Buddhist stūpas in various places;
how can this country suddenly obtain so many?
Thereupon, the king spoke to the people with skillful means.
"I shall now remit for you thirty-five million taels of gold.
He further declared, "Whether a kingdom possesses many stupas or few,
from this day forward, all are permitted to no longer pay gold to me."
Eventually, King Aśoka went to the place where the venerable Arhat Yaśas was staying and said,
"I wish to erect eighty-four thousand stūpas in a single day and a single thought-moment, so that they may all be completed simultaneously."
And he spoke in verse:
"From among the seven previous reliquaries, I, the king of the Maurya clan, have constructed [this stūpa] in a single day, taking the relics of the World-Honored One."
The eighty-four thousand stupas were as radiant as white clouds;
even until King Aśoka had erected the eighty-four thousand stupas and was protecting the Buddha-dharma, the people called him the Dharma-king Aśoka.
All the people of the world spoke in verse:
"The Great Sage, King of Peacocks, Knowing the Dharma, brings great benefit;
By means of the stūpa seal, he adorns the world And casts away evil names upon the earth."
Attaining a good reputation as the Dharma King, one finds peace and happiness through the Dharma.

The Aśokarāja-sūtra, Scroll One. Translated on the twentieth day of the sixth month in the eleventh year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty by the Śramaṇa Saṃghabara of Fushan at the Shouguang Hall in Yangdu.
Recorded in the Baochang lu. The Aśokarāja-sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabara of Funan during the Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Two: The Account of Seeing Upagupta. Chapter Two: The Account of Seeing Upagupta.
At that time, King Aśoka...
Having erected eighty-four thousand stūpas for the relics, he was filled with great joy.
Together with his ministers, he went to the Kukkuta Monastery;
having arrived, he joined his palms in reverence before the Elder and spoke these words:
The Buddha, the All-Seeing One, prophesied that because I offered sand to the Buddha, I have now obtained this retribution.
"Are there any others whom the Buddha has likewise prophesied?
At that time, the Elder Bhikṣu named Yaśas (translated as "Renowned") replied to King Aśoka, saying, "There are."
Before the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, there was a nāga king named Aparāntaka (translated as "No-Remainder"),
as well as a potter and a caṇḍāla (translated as "Evil" nāga kings).
After the Buddha had thus transformed these beings, he arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā.
In Mathurā, he addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying:
"In this kingdom of Mathurā, one hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa..."
There will be a merchant leader of incense named Gupta.
Later, he will father a son named Upagupta,
who will be the most excellent teacher as a Buddha without marks (animitta-buddha).
"After my parinirvāṇa, I shall perform the work of a Buddha.
He further addressed Ānanda: "Do you now see that distant green forest?
Ānanda replied, "I have seen it."
The Buddha said, "There is a mountain there named Urumanda.
One hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
a monastery shall be established upon that mountain."
It was named Natabhata, the most excellent place for meditative seclusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Among those who teach disciples, his wisdom is foremost."
"The World-Honored One has prophesied that the venerable Upagupta shall extensively perform the work of a Buddha in this world.
At that time, King Aśoka again questioned the Elder Yaśas.
Upagupta asked, "Is he already born, Great Virtue?
Yaśas replied, "He has already been born on Mount Urubilvā;
he has eliminated all afflictions."
All the Arhats follow him and sustain the world; therefore,
just as the Omniscient One does for devas, humans, asuras, nāgas,
spirits, and others, he preaches the Dharma to them.
At that time, the Elder Upagupta was surrounded by eighteen thousand arhats at the Nandapada Monastery.
Then King Aśoka spoke these verses to his ministers:
"You should quickly prepare the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry."
I wish to go to that country, to Mount Urumanda,
desiring to see the Great Virtuous One named Upagupta,
who is diligent and energetic, has exhausted all outflows, and has attained arhatship.
Then the ministers said to King Aśoka,
"Your Majesty should send a messenger to inform those people that Upagupta is to come to the king's gate.
The king replied to the ministers.
"One who is an Arhat must not be treated with contempt; we should now go in person to pay him homage.
Then he spoke this verse:
"Dwelling in the world like the Tathāgata, He is named Upagupta."
If he does not accept his instruction, his mind will become like adamant;
even King Aśoka sent an envoy to Upagupta’s residence and addressed Upagupta, saying:
"I wish to go to the place where the Great Virtuous One resides.
Having heard the messenger's words, Upagupta reflected:
"If King Aśoka comes, he will surely be followed by many attendants, and they shall bring ruin to this country."
Having reflected thus, he spoke to the messenger, saying, "I shall go there myself;
it is not necessary for the king to come. The king then had ships constructed to welcome Upagupta and ensured that every road along the way was thoroughly repaired and prepared.
Upon arriving at the kingdom of Mathurā, Upagupta led eighteen thousand arhats;
for the sake of supporting King Aśoka, they all boarded ships and traveled as far as the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. At that time, the subjects of King Aśoka addressed the Great King, saying:
Upagupta has come to this country in order to take the King under his care; Great King,
you should know that the Buddha-dharma is like the earth.
"Your Majesty now cultivates goodness; by means of this, you shall attain the correct crossing of the ocean of the three realms of existence and reach the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Upagupta will arrive at your palace on foot tomorrow morning."
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and immediately took off a necklace worth ten million pieces of gold to reward the man.
He further ordered the man to beat the drums and proclaim a decree so that everyone throughout the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra would know that Upagupta would enter the country the following day.
Furthermore, he caused this person to recite these verses:
"If one desires wealth and happiness, As well as the causes for rebirth in heaven and liberation,
One should see all of these In that Upagupta."
If a person does not see the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings,
the self-arisen one of great compassion, the stainless Great Teacher—
such a person should instead make offerings to Upagupta, who is equal to him.
He went so far as to cause King Aśoka to have all the people hear these verses and further to have the roads prepared and adorned.
At that time, the king went out of the city for half a yojana, accompanied by his ministers and citizens,
solemnly holding incense and flowers and performing various kinds of music to welcome Upagupta.
Then King Aśoka saw from afar that Upagupta had already reached the shore.
Accompanied by eighteen thousand arhats who surrounded him like the shape of a half-moon,
he immediately dismounted from his elephant and proceeded on foot to where Upagupta was.
At that time, King Aśoka stood with one foot on the boat and one foot on the shore;
cupping Upagupta with both hands, he placed him within the boat and prostrated himself before his feet,
falling to the ground like a great tree broken and cast down.
Furthermore, licking his two feet with his tongue, he knelt for a long time with palms joined, gazing up at him without weariness, and spoke this verse: "The great earth,
clothed by the oceans, adorned by mountains, and crowned by a single parasol— having eliminated all enmity,
you have attained this ground, which brings me great joy."
It is not as good as meeting a virtuous one today;
now that I have seen this virtuous one, my mindfulness increases twofold.
Therefore, joy arises within me, for I have seen the World-Honored One.
The Buddha has already entered nirvāṇa; you, O Great Virtuous One, perform the work of a Buddha.
For this world shrouded in ignorance, you are like the light of the sun and moon;
adorned with wisdom, you are truly equal to the Great Teacher.
The foremost teacher of men, the refuge of all sentient beings— I should see him as one to be taught;
I shall act according to his instructions.
At that time, the Venerable Upagupta...
He stroked King Aśoka’s head with his right hand and spoke this verse:
“O King, you have now attained sovereignty; you should now practice heedfulness.”
The encounter with the Triple Gem is difficult to find; Your Majesty should always make offerings.
The World-Honored One has entrusted the Dharma-treasury to you and us;
you should protect the Buddha-dharma for the sake of gathering in and sustaining sentient beings.
King Aśoka replied,
"As the World-Honored One prophesied,
I have now fulfilled it," and he spoke this verse:
I have now made offerings to the relics and images of the World-Honored One,
and have erected stūpas everywhere, adorned with precious jewels;
yet I alone am unable to leave the household life to practice the holy life.
Upagupta said, "Great King, excellent,
excellent! Such a matter as this is precisely what a king ought to do."
For what reason?
A king, regarding his body, life, and wealth, should practice true reality;
if the king is in another world, he shall not undergo the sufferings of that other world.
Then King Aśoka, with great offerings,
escorted Upagupta into the city;
he received the Venerable One in his own hands and placed him upon a high seat.
The body of Upagupta was as soft and supple as *tūla* cotton.
When King Aśoka touched his body, he joined his palms and said:
"Venerable One, your body is as soft and supple as Kāśī cotton."
"Now my body is coarse and rough," [he said]. When he touched the body of the Great Virtuous One, Upagupta spoke again in verse:
"With this supreme offering, I make an offering to the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
When the King offered sand to the Tathāgata,
King Aśoka again spoke in verse:
"With the mind of a small child, I formerly offered sand to the World-Honored One."
Having encountered a field of merit,
Upagupta now acts as the king's counselor in order to inspire joy in Aśoka.
And he spoke these verses:
"The King encountered a field of merit And sowed the seeds of generosity;
Therefore he has obtained this retribution, Inconceivable bliss."
Having heard this, the king’s heart was filled with great joy,
and he spoke again in verse:
"In the past, I gave sand as an offering To the World-Honored One, the Great Field of Merit."
"Now I have attained incomparable bliss;
who, upon hearing such a matter, would not make offerings to the Tathāgata?
At that time, King Aśoka prostrated at the feet of Upagupta and said:
"Venerable Sir, I wish to make offerings at all places where the Buddha walked, stood, sat, and remained.
Furthermore, I wish to create signs so that future sentient beings may know the locations where the Buddha Tathāgata walked, stood, sat, and lay down."
To effect their gathering, he spoke these verses:
"I desire to perform offerings at every place where the Tathāgata has walked, stood, sat,
or lain, in order to leave behind the suffering of birth and death."
Furthermore, wishing to manifest the postures of the Tathāgata— walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—
to serve as the conditions for future sentient beings to give rise to the vision of the Buddha,
Upagupta replied:
"Great King, excellent, excellent! This mind of yours is most difficult to surpass.
I now wish to manifest for you, Great King, the four modes of deportment of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, so that you may perceive his marks."
Desiring to gather in and sustain all sentient beings,
King Aśoka then arrayed his fourfold army and,
accompanied by fragrant flowers and musical performances, set out with Upagupta.
Upon arriving at that place, Upagupta led King Aśoka to the Buddha’s birthplace; entering the Lumbinī Grove—the site of liberation—he raised his right hand and said:
King Aśoka said:
"This is the birthplace of the Buddha," and he spoke this verse:
The World-Honored One, in his first station, As soon as born, took seven steps;
With pure eyes he surveyed the four quarters, And uttered a lion’s roar:
“This is my final birth; My dwelling in the womb was likewise so.”
Then King Aśoka prostrated himself on the ground with his five limbs,
bowed his head at the place where the Tathāgata was born,
and with palms joined, spoke this verse:
Those who see the Buddha are endowed with great merit;
likewise, those who hear the lion’s roar possess such merit.
Upagupta inspired great faith in King Aśoka.
He then asked the king,
"There are those who have seen the Buddha when he was first born and took seven steps,
as well as those who heard his lion’s roar; would Your Majesty wish to see him?"
The King replied, "Venerable Sir, I now wish to see Upagupta. [Upagupta said:
"When the Tathāgata was first born, Queen Māyā grasped the branch of a tree, and a deity was within it."
Even as he pointed out the location with his hand,
he spoke this verse:
"If there are any devas or humans dwelling within this forest..."
Having seen the birth of the World-Honored One and heard his lion’s roar,
he manifested his own body to inspire faith in Aśoka;
at that moment, the deva revealed his form.
Standing before Upagupta with palms joined, he said,
"Venerable Sir, what should I do?
Then Upagupta spoke to King Aśoka.
When this deva saw the Buddha’s birth,
King Aśoka joined his palms toward the deva and spoke this verse:
You have seen the Buddha at his birth, his body adorned with a hundred merits;
his face like a lotus flower, beloved by all the world.
Furthermore, you have heard his lion’s roar here within this great forest.
At that time, the deva replied with a verse:
"I have seen the Buddha’s body, Its radiance like the color of gold;
Walking seven paces through the air, The most supreme among two-legged beings."
I also heard the lion’s roar when he was the Honored One among gods and humans.
At that time, the King asked:
"What auspicious signs appeared at the time of the Tathāgata’s birth?"
The deva replied:
"I am now unable to describe these wondrous matters in detail;
I shall speak only a small portion."
Then he spoke in verse:
He emits golden light, Which illuminates the blind world,
Bringing joy to gods and humans alike, And causing the mountains, seas, and earth to tremble.
Even until the time of King Aśoka,
he offered one hundred thousand *tolas* of gold at the place where the Tathāgata was born,
immediately erected a stūpa there, and then proceeded to other locations.
Then Upagupta led King Aśoka to the dwelling place of the ṛṣi Kapilavastu, which was greenish-blue in color;
raising his hand, he pointed it out to the king, saying, "This is that place."
People presented the Bodhisattva to King Śuklodana.
Adorned with the thirty-two marks and a lovely complexion, his body was magnificently arrayed.
Upon seeing him, the king prostrated himself before him, casting down his five limbs in worship.
Śākyamuni’s clan name was Bhadana, which translates as "Righteous"; it was a place where celestial deities resided.
When the Bodhisattva arrived there intending to pay homage to the deity, the deity did not accept his prostration at that time.
And they paid homage to the Bodhisattva.
At that time, King Śuklodana, having witnessed this event, immediately said:
"This son of mine is now the god of gods."
He immediately gave it a name, calling it "Devadatta.
Furthermore, he said, "This is the place where the Brahmin physiognomist examined the Bodhisattva," and he also said,
"This is the place where the rishi prophesied concerning the Bodhisattva."
It is said that after this child was born, he was destined to become a Buddha.
It is further said that this is the place where Mahāprajāpatī raised the Bodhisattva,
and it is also said that this is the place where the Bodhisattva studied writing.
Furthermore, it is said that this is the place where Bodhisattvas practice various arts and skills, such as riding elephants, chariots, and horses;
it is also said that this is the place where Bodhisattvas reach the ultimate fulfillment of all paths.
Furthermore, it is said that this is the place where the Bodhisattva turned the stone wheel;
it is also said that this is the place where he enjoyed himself with sixty thousand court ladies;
and it is further said that this is the place where the Bodhisattva, upon witnessing old age, sickness, and death, gave rise to a heart of compassion.

Furthermore, it is said that this is where the Bodhisattva, beneath the Jambu tree, cultivated various meditative concentrations, detached from desires and unwholesome states, and entered the first dhyāna,
which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and characterized by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
When the Bodhisattva sat in meditation, the day having already passed midday, the shadow of the Bodhi tree did not shift;
the shadows of all other trees, however, turned with the sun.
At that time, King Śuklodana, witnessing this phenomenon, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and paid homage at the feet of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there were ten thousand devas and humans here who followed and attended upon the Bodhisattva as he departed from the city of Kapilavastu in the middle of the night.
Moreover, this is the place where the Bodhisattva removed his jeweled crown and sent the horse and Chandaka back.
And he spoke in verse:
"Having cast off my jeweled crown and necklaces, along with the horse and Chandaka, I bid them return to their native land; I remain alone, without attendants."
To cultivate the practice of diligent effort, the Bodhisattva entered the mountains to study the Way; at this place,
he exchanged his Kāśī robes for the saffron robe of a hunter and then went forth into homelessness.
This is the place where Śarabhaṅga, translated as "Surname," invited the Bodhisattva.
This is the place where Bimbisāra, translated as "King Who Embraces Reality," gave half his kingdom to the Bodhisattva.
This is the place where he questioned Udraka Rāmaputra and further spoke in verse.
In this place dwelt a seer named Udraka Rāmaputra;
having heard his doctrine, [the Bodhisattva] departed. O King of Men, here you practiced austerities for six years, without any other teacher.
Again, he spoke in verse:
"For six years I practiced asceticism, A difficult path that I have already known;
I realized that asceticism is not the Way, And thus I abandoned the practices of the sages."
This is the place where the Bodhisattva received the sixteen-fold milk-rice offered by the two sisters, Nandā and Nandabalā; having accepted it, he ate it and then spoke these verses.
In this place, the Bodhisattva, the Great Hero of Supreme Speech, partook of the milk-rice offered by Nanda; it was here, between the Bodhi trees,
that the Nāga King Kāli praised the Bodhisattva.
As stated in the verse:
"The dragon king named Kāli, having offered praise, spoke these words:
'By this path one shall proceed to the site of the Bodhi tree.'"
At that time, King Aśoka prostrated at the feet of Upagupta, joined his palms, and said:
"I wish to see the Nāga King, who previously beheld the Tathāgata walking like an elephant king."
Proceeding along this path toward the Bodhi tree,
Upagupta went to the dwelling of Kālī and spoke these verses with his finger:
"O most excellent among dragon kings, you should now manifest your body;
you shall behold the conduct of the Bodhisattva as he proceeds toward the Tree of Enlightenment.
At that time, the Dragon King Kāli immediately manifested his form.
Joining his palms before Upagupta, he said,
"Venerable Sir, what should I do?
Upagupta spoke to King Aśoka, saying:
This was the Dragon King Kāli who offered praise when the Bodhisattva proceeded along this path toward the Bodhi tree. At that time,
King Aśoka joined his palms in reverence toward the Dragon King Kāli.
And he spoke in verse:
"You behold the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Whose radiance is like the color of gold,
Unequaled in the world, With a face like the full moon of autumn."
"O you who possess the great merit of the ten powers, you should speak even a single portion [of it].
How does one proceed from this practice? The Dragon King Kāli, endowed with the Buddha's spiritual power, replied:
I cannot explain this in detail now, but shall speak briefly; O King, listen attentively as I recite these verses:
"When the Bodhisattva treads upon the earth, The six great elements tremble, As do the great oceans and all the mountains, Emitting a radiance that surpasses the sun."
When King Aśoka had finished erecting a stūpa at the abode of the Nāga king and was about to depart,
Upagupta took King Aśoka to the Bodhi tree and, pointing his finger, said:
"Great King, at this place, the Bodhisattva, taking compassion as his companion, conquered the army of Māra.
Having awakened to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
he spoke these verses:"
When the King Tuṣita, having satisfied various hosts of Māras and attained the incomparable *amṛta* of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
King Aśoka made an offering of one hundred thousand pieces of gold to the Bodhi tree.
Once the stūpa had been erected, they departed.
Upagupta then addressed the king again, saying,
"This is the place where the Buddha accepted the four alms-bowls from the Four Heavenly Kings and joined them into one."
Furthermore, at this place, the Buddha accepted the food offered by the two merchant leaders, Trapusa and Bhallika.
From this location, the Buddha proceeded to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Upagupta who praised the dwelling place of the Tathāgata.
Upagupta then led King Aśoka to the site of Ṛṣipatana and, pointing his finger, said:
"This is the place where the World-Honored One turned the Wheel of Dharma three times in twelve aspects."
Then he spoke in verse:
"This is the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned thrice, In twelve aspects,
composed of the true Dharma, For the sake of crossing over the suffering of birth and death."
This is the place where one thousand non-Buddhist renunciants went forth.
Furthermore, this is the place where the Buddha preached the Dharma for King Bimbisāra, enabling him to realize the Truth;

and water issued from the lower part of his body while fire issued from the upper part.
Even unto employing various supernormal powers,
he caused his fellow students and all beings born as humans to give rise to great joy and attain liberation of mind;
he then entered nirvana, like water extinguishing fire.
He then used these tally-sticks to cremate his body,
and even erected a stupa and made various offerings to it.
This was when Upagupta entered nirvana.
Furthermore, one thousand arhats passed away and entered nirvana; finally,
even Xi Zhengke, having completed his protection of the Dharma-treasury, entered nirvana.
The account of Upagupta is concluded.
The True Dharma shall abide for a long time without perishing; the stūpas containing the śarīra relics shall likewise remain.
This person who upholds the Dharma shall cherish it without end.
It is likewise eternally abiding and indestructible,
from the time of King Aśoka’s causal conditions until Upagupta entered nirvāṇa.
In the foreign land, there were a total of three thousand one hundred verses.
Each verse consisted of thirty-two syllables.
There were twenty-eight disciples.
